evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected acute appendicitis in the emergency department (paediatric and pregnancy points noted). Verified against the WSES Jerusalem guidelines 2020 update and the Saudi MOH Intra-abdominal Infections Treatment Protocol (antibiotic choice and duration).
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Preoperative prophylaxis agent — local surgical prophylaxis protocol

pathophysiology.summary: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, usually after luminal obstruction (faecolith/appendicolith or lymphoid hyperplasia). Rising pressure causes venous congestion, ischaemia and bacterial invasion of the wall; untreated, it can become gangrenous and perforate, forming a phlegmon, abscess or generalised peritonitis.
keyMechanisms: Visceral (midgut) pain from appendiceal distension is felt periumbilically; when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum the pain localises to the right iliac fossa.
Uncomplicated appendicitis: inflamed without gangrene, perforation or abscess — may resolve with antibiotics (or even spontaneously) in selected patients.
Complicated appendicitis: gangrene, perforation, phlegmon or periappendiceal abscess; an appendicolith predicts failure of non-operative treatment.
Appendiceal neoplasms are found in 3–17% of adults aged 40 or over with complicated appendicitis (WSES).

symptoms: Abdominal pain starting centrally and moving to the right iliac fossa.
Atypical presentations in older adults, pregnancy (pain may be higher) and children.
physicalSigns: Right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding and rebound (peritonism).
Generalised peritonitis, sepsis or a palpable mass (phlegmon/abscess) in complicated disease.
redFlags: Pregnancy (do not diagnose on symptoms alone; non-operative treatment not advised)
Age 40 or over with complicated disease — consider underlying neoplasm
precipitants: Rarely tumour (carcinoid, mucinous neoplasm) — especially age 40 or over.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and risk-stratify
actions: Analgesia (do not withhold for diagnosis); IV fluids if dehydrated; nil by mouth if surgery likely.
Calculate AIR or AAS score: low risk — consider discharge with safety-netting; intermediate — observe and image; high risk — surgical review.

clinicalManagement.title: Image when indicated
actions: Ultrasound (POCUS by an experienced operator) first.
Negative or inconclusive ultrasound and still intermediate risk: low-dose contrast CT (adults); MRI in pregnancy.
High risk and under 40: may go straight to diagnostic ± therapeutic laparoscopy.

clinicalManagement.title: Uncomplicated appendicitis
actions: Laparoscopic appendectomy on the next available list, within 24 h (do not delay beyond 24 h).
Single preoperative dose of broad-spectrum antibiotic 0–60 min before incision; NO postoperative antibiotics.
Antibiotic-first (non-operative) option: discuss with selected patients without an appendicolith — recurrence up to 39% at 5 years; start IV then switch to oral. Not advised in pregnancy.

clinicalManagement.title: Complicated appendicitis (gangrene, perforation, peritonitis)
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Urgently — within 8 h in children (WSES); source control within 24 h (MOH)
actions: Start antibiotics in the ED after cultures: ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 h + metronidazole 500 mg IV/PO every 8 h (other MOH Table 2 options below).
Severe infection, septic shock, older or immunocompromised: piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 h or meropenem 1 g IV every 8 h (MOH).
Laparoscopic appendectomy; suction only (no irrigation); no routine drains in adults; routine histopathology.
Postoperative antibiotics: stop after 3–5 days if source control is adequate (WSES); MOH: 24 h if operated within 12–24 h, 4 days with adequate source control. Switch to oral when eating.
Follow the sepsis pathway; antibiotics within the first hour; urgent source control.

clinicalManagement.title: Phlegmon or periappendiceal abscess
actions: Non-operative management with antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage is reasonable first-line, especially without advanced laparoscopic expertise.
Laparoscopic surgery is a safe alternative in experienced hands.
No routine interval appendectomy in under-40s; age 40 or over treated non-operatively: colonoscopy and interval contrast CT (neoplasm risk).

keyPoints: Use AIR or AAS score to stratify; Alvarado cannot confirm appendicitis in adults.
Ultrasound first; low-dose CT if still unsure.
Laparoscopic appendectomy within 24 h; earlier if complicated.
One preop antibiotic dose for uncomplicated; 3–5 days or less after source control for complicated.
Pregnancy test in every woman of reproductive age.
pitfalls: Antibiotic-only treatment with an appendicolith or in pregnancy.
Missing a tumour in patients 40 or over treated non-operatively.
Discharging an intermediate-risk patient without imaging or review.

patientEducation: Wound care and return warning signs after surgery.
lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
mdtReferrals: General surgery for all suspected appendicitis above low risk.
Interventional radiology for drainable abscess; obstetrics in pregnancy.
dischargeCriteria: Low-risk score with no peritonism, tolerating oral intake, pain controlled, reliable return advice (non-operated).
After surgery: eating, mobile, pain controlled on oral analgesia, afebrile.
Non-operative treatment: clinically improving on oral antibiotics.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Return immediately if pain worsens, fever or vomiting. Non-operative patients: warn of recurrence. Age 40 or over treated non-operatively: colonoscopy and interval CT. Review histopathology.

adjustments: Alternatives (MOH Table 2): cefuroxime 1.5 g IV q8h or cefotaxime 2 g IV q8h + metronidazole; single agents ertapenem 1 g IV q24h or piperacillin–tazobactam 3.375 g IV q6h
Severe beta-lactam allergy: ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h or levofloxacin 750 mg q24h + metronidazole

medicationPlan.note: Antibiotic doses from the Saudi MOH Intra-abdominal Infections Treatment Protocol; follow the local antibiogram. WSES does not specify the preoperative prophylaxis agent — use the hospital surgical prophylaxis protocol.
